chapter_seo_title: Dao Guai Yi Xian Chapter 297 — A drunken feast with Tuoba reveals the true currency of the Office: lifespan itself.
chapter_meta_description: Li Huowang bonds with Tuoba Danqing over wine and boasts, only to discover the casual horror of a Heart-Element specimen pulled from a burlap sack.
og_title: Chapter 297: Treasure — A Drink With the Monster Next Door
og_description: Li Huowang enjoys a fancy dinner and learns the Supervisory Heavenly Office trades in years of life—then watches Tuoba Danqing pull a Heart-Element head from a bag.
twitter_description: Drinks, bonding, then a severed head full of organs. Just another Tuesday in the Dao-Twisted World.

lore_anchors.definition: In Chinese folk religion, a person's allotted lifespan, conceived as a finite resource that can be spent, traded, or stolen; the Supervisory Heavenly Office uses it as official currency.
A rare human constitution that makes its bearer a prime alchemical ingredient; the novel treats it as a cosmological anomaly that attracts predators from every corner of the Dao-Twisted World.
A multi-storied, intricately carved pagoda; in Chinese architecture, "Linglong" denotes exquisite craftsmanship, often associated with Buddhist or Daoist sacred sites.
The name of the ruling dynasty in the Dao-Twisted World; its existence grounds the supernatural horror in a pseudo-historical political framework.
A Daoist term for the celestial realm of the highest immortals; a toast "to early ascent to the Crimson Palace" is a blessing for rapid immortal advancement.

cultural_notes_faq.q: What is "yang life" and why is it used as currency?
cultural_notes_faq.a: In the Dao-Twisted World, yang life (阳寿) represents a person's remaining lifespan. The Supervisory Heavenly Office uses it as its official medium of exchange, making every transaction a literal life-or-death matter.

cultural_notes_faq.q: Why does Tuoba Danqing casually pull out a severed head during a friendly dinner?
cultural_notes_faq.a: Because the Dao-Twisted World normalizes such savagery. What is a trophy to Tuoba is a nightmare symptom to Li Huowang—and the casual reveal serves to remind both the protagonist and the reader that no institution in this world is truly benign.

In standard Daoist cosmology, heaven (Qian, ☰) should be above earth (Kun, ☷) to represent order. A reversed trigram artifact places Kun above Qian, symbolizing inverted, corrupted, or "upside-down" power—a hallmark of Zuowandao theft and the Dao-Twisted World's abnormal nature.
